Cattle
KAT-'l
n. (rendering Hebrew b'hēmâh and miqneh, Greek ktēnos)
From Old French catel, from Latin capitale, property or capital — the same root that gives English chattel, since in an agrarian society a man's herds simply were his capital. The Hebrew miqneh makes the identical connection from the other direction: it is formed from qānâh, to acquire, so that cattle are literally acquisitions. B'hēmâh is the wider word for beasts, particularly domestic ones, as distinguished from the wild beast of the field.

Biblical Definition

Cattle appear on the sixth day, made before man and pronounced good in their own right: “And God made the beast of the earth after his kind, and cattle after their kind, and every thing that creepeth upon the earth after his kind: and God saw that it was good” (Gen 1:25). The verdict is given before man exists to make use of them, which establishes that their goodness is not a function of their usefulness. Ownership of them is God's and not the herdsman's, and the psalm states it in a line that has become proverbial: “For every beast of the forest is mine, and the cattle upon a thousand hills” (Psa 50:10) — spoken to men who imagined they were supplying God by sacrifice. Because the cattle are God's, they are covered by His law, and the fourth commandment extends the sabbath rest to them explicitly: “thou shalt not do any work, thou, nor thy son, nor thy daughter, thy manservant, nor thy maidservant, nor thy cattle, nor thy stranger that is within thy gates” (Exo 20:10). The beast gets the day off, and the law that protects him is the same law that governs the household. Most striking of all is the last sentence of Jonah, where God ends His argument with the sulking prophet by naming the animals: should not I spare Nineveh, wherein are more than sixscore thousand persons that cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand, “and also much cattle?” (Jon 4:11). The mercy of God, closing the book, takes in the herds.

Webster 1828 Definition

Beasts or quadrupeds kept for tillage, food, or profit — oxen, sheep, and the like; in Scripture the domestic beasts made good on the sixth day, owned by God upon a thousand hills, given rest by the fourth commandment, and named in God's mercy over Nineveh.

expand to see more

CATTLE, n. 1. Beasts or quadrupeds in general, serving for tillage, or other labor, or for food to man.

2. In its primary sense, the word includes camels, horses, asses, and all the varieties of domestic animals.

3. In the United States, it is applied chiefly to bovine animals, as oxen, bulls, cows and their young.

4. In the Hebrew, from a root signifying to acquire; possessions or substance, the herds being the wealth of a pastoral people.

5. In Scripture, the cattle upon a thousand hills. Psalm 50. Nor thy cattle. Exod. 20. And also much cattle. Jonah 4.

Key Scripture

Genesis 1:25 — "And God made the beast of the earth after his kind, and cattle after their kind, and every thing that creepeth upon the earth after his kind: and God saw that it was good."

Psalm 50:10 — "For every beast of the forest is mine, and the cattle upon a thousand hills."

Exodus 20:10 — "But the seventh day is the sabbath of the LORD thy God: in it thou shalt not do any work, thou, nor thy son, nor thy daughter, thy manservant, nor thy maidservant, nor thy cattle, nor thy stranger that is within thy gates:"

Jonah 4:11 — "And should not I spare Nineveh, that great city, wherein are more than sixscore thousand persons that cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand; and also much cattle?"

Modern Corruption

Animals are either elevated to the moral standing of persons, so that human dominion is treated as tyranny, or reduced to pure commodity, so that the creature's good is nothing and cruelty costs nothing.

expand to see more

The first corruption abolishes the creational distinction between man and beast. Where animals are granted rights identical to human rights, or where human beings are described as merely one species among others with no special standing, Scripture is directly contradicted: only man is made in the image of God, only man is given dominion, and only for man did the Son of God become incarnate. The Lord Jesus settles the comparison plainly — are ye not much better than they? and, how much then is a man better than a sheep? To flatten that distinction is not compassion but confusion, and in practice it has repeatedly coincided with a diminished regard for human life rather than an enlarged regard for animal life.

The opposite corruption is the commercial one, and among the orthodox it is by far the commoner. Because man has dominion, it is inferred that the beast has no claim at all — that stewardship means unlimited use. Scripture says otherwise and legislates against it: a righteous man regardeth the life of his beast; the ox is not to be muzzled while he treads out the corn; the beast rests on the sabbath; the fallen animal of even an enemy must be helped up. The principle to recover is that dominion is a trust exercised under an Owner who declares the cattle upon a thousand hills to be His, and who ends the book of Jonah by naming the herds among the reasons for sparing a city. Cruelty to an animal is not an offence against the animal's rights; it is an offence against its Maker's.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew b'hēmâh is a beast, especially a domestic one; miqneh is cattle as acquired property, from qānâh, to acquire; bāqār is the herd of oxen. Greek ktēnos is a beast of burden or property.

expand to see more

Hebrew b'hēmâh (H929) — beast, cattle; the domestic animals as distinct from chayyâh, the wild beast of the field.

Hebrew miqneh (H4735) — cattle as possession or substance; from qānâh, to acquire or purchase, whence a man's herds are his capital.

Hebrew bāqār (H1241) — the herd, oxen; distinguished from tsō'n, the flock of sheep and goats.

Greek ktēnos (G2934) — a beast of burden or domestic animal, from ktaomai, to acquire; the beast on which the wounded man was set (Luk 10:34).

Hebrew b'hēmōth — the intensive plural of b'hēmâh, used in Job 40:15 of the great beast God bids Job consider.

Usage

"Of their creation and goodness: God made... cattle after their kind... and God saw that it was good (Gen 1:25)."

"Of God's ownership: every beast of the forest is mine, and the cattle upon a thousand hills (Psa 50:10)."

"Of sabbath rest extended to them: thou shalt not do any work... nor thy cattle (Exo 20:10)."
